name: The Paxos Algorithm
statement: Get unreliable machines to agree on one value, keeping consistency even when some fail.
statementAccent: keeping consistency even when some fail
meaning: Paxos is a family of protocols for solving consensus in a network of unreliable or fallible processors. Consensus is the problem of getting a group of distributed processes to agree on a single value, or a sequence of values, even in the presence of failures such as crashes, lost messages, and delays. Paxos guarantees safety, that is, consistency: the processes never disagree on the chosen value, and this holds even under asynchronous conditions and failures. It is designed to tolerate crash faults, not Byzantine ones; it assumes that processes may fail by stopping and that messages may be lost or delayed, but not that processes lie or act maliciously, so basic Paxos is not Byzantine fault tolerant. Progress, or liveness, is not guaranteed under all conditions, consistent with the famous FLP impossibility result that no deterministic asynchronous consensus protocol can guarantee both safety and liveness in the presence of even a single faulty process. Paxos assigns roles to processes: proposers propose values, acceptors vote on proposed values, and learners learn the chosen value; a value is chosen when a majority, or quorum, of acceptors accept it, and the protocol proceeds in numbered proposals across two phases, prepare and promise, then accept and accepted. It was devised by Leslie Lamport, who described it through an analogy to the part-time parliament of a fictional ancient Greek island called Paxos; his paper The Part-Time Parliament was published in 1998, and Paxos Made Simple restated it in 2001. Famously hard to understand, Paxos motivated the more approachable Raft algorithm. It underlies fault-tolerant systems such as Google's Chubby and Spanner.
mechanism: Paxos coordinates a set of unreliable processes so they agree on one value despite crashes, message loss, and delay, and it guarantees that once a value is chosen no process ever sees a different one. It divides responsibilities among roles. Proposers put forward values; acceptors are the voting members whose accumulated acceptances actually choose a value; and learners find out what was chosen. The safety of the protocol rests on majorities: because any two majorities of acceptors overlap in at least one acceptor, no two different values can each be accepted by a majority, which is what prevents disagreement. Paxos proceeds through numbered proposals in two phases. In the first phase, a proposer selects a proposal number and sends a prepare request to the acceptors; each acceptor, if it has not already promised to ignore that number, replies with a promise not to accept any lower-numbered proposal and reports any value it has already accepted. In the second phase, if the proposer hears promises from a majority, it sends an accept request carrying a value, either its own or, crucially, the value from the highest-numbered proposal any of those acceptors reported, and acceptors that have not since promised a higher number accept it. Once a majority accepts, the value is chosen, and learners are informed. The numbering and the two-phase discipline ensure that later proposals defer to values already chosen, preserving consistency even when proposers compete or fail mid-protocol. Paxos handles crash faults and lost messages but assumes no lying, so it is not Byzantine tolerant, and it cannot guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system, in line with the FLP result; in practice a single elected leader, or distinguished proposer, is used to make progress reliable.

examples.text: Proposers propose, acceptors vote, and learners learn; a value is chosen when a majority of acceptors accept it.
Because any two majorities of acceptors share a member, two different values cannot both be chosen.
A prepare-and-promise phase is followed by an accept-and-accepted phase, using numbered proposals.

whyItMatters: Paxos is a landmark of distributed computing, the protocol that showed how a collection of unreliable machines can nonetheless agree, reliably and consistently, on shared decisions, and it is the theoretical backbone of fault-tolerant distributed systems. Consensus, getting distributed processes to agree despite failures, is one of the deepest problems in the field, and it is the foundation of replicated state machines, the standard technique for building services that stay correct and available even when individual servers crash. Paxos gives a rigorous, proven solution: it guarantees that agreement, once reached, is never contradicted, no matter how messages are lost or reordered or how processes fail by stopping, which is exactly the safety property that critical infrastructure requires. This has made Paxos and its variants the engine of some of the most important distributed systems ever built, including Google's Chubby lock service and Spanner database, and it inspired closely related protocols such as ZooKeeper's Zab. Paxos is also famous for its difficulty: Lamport's whimsical presentation as an ancient parliament and the protocol's subtlety made it notoriously hard to understand and implement, which directly motivated the design of Raft as a more approachable alternative with the same guarantees. Its relationship to the FLP impossibility result also illuminates the fundamental limits of asynchronous agreement. As the protocol that makes unreliable machines agree on one value while preserving consistency, Paxos is foundational to reliable distributed systems.

working.text: a proposer sends a numbered prepare request, and acceptors promise not to accept lower-numbered proposals.
on a majority of promises, the proposer sends an accept request, respecting any already-accepted value.
once a majority accepts a value it is chosen, and learners are informed, with overlap guaranteeing consistency.

limits: Paxos is rigorous but bounded, and several points reward care. It guarantees safety, never disagreeing on the chosen value, but not liveness: in a fully asynchronous system it cannot guarantee that it will ever terminate, exactly as the FLP impossibility result requires, and competing proposers can in principle prevent progress indefinitely, which is why practical deployments elect a single leader to make progress reliable. Paxos tolerates crash faults and lost or delayed messages but assumes processes do not lie or act maliciously, so it is not Byzantine fault tolerant; systems facing adversarial participants need Byzantine protocols instead. It is also notoriously difficult to understand and to implement correctly, and the gap between the abstract single-value protocol and a working multi-value replicated system, Multi-Paxos, is substantial, a difficulty that motivated Raft. Some details reward care: Paxos requires a majority quorum of acceptors, its safety rests on the overlap of majorities, Lamport's papers are The Part-Time Parliament in 1998 and Paxos Made Simple in 2001, and ZooKeeper's Zab is Paxos-like but distinct rather than Paxos itself. So Paxos robustly guarantees consistent consensus among crash-prone machines, understood as safe but not always live, crash- not Byzantine-tolerant, and famously hard to implement.
misreadings: Paxos does not guarantee progress, only consistency; in an asynchronous system it may fail to terminate, as the FLP result requires. It does not tolerate lying or malicious processes, being crash-fault-tolerant, not Byzantine. And it is subtle to implement, not a plug-in recipe, so treating Paxos as guaranteeing liveness, as surviving Byzantine faults, or as trivial to build, misreads it.
origin: The consensus protocol devised by Leslie Lamport, presented as an ancient Greek parliament in papers of 1998 and 2001, which lets unreliable crash-prone processes agree on a value while preserving consistency.
